cases.n: Victoria — Board of Inquiry into historical child sexual abuse at Beaumaris Primary School and other government schools (2024)
cases.victims_note: the board said the four teachers it focused on are believed to have abused more than 100 students; more than 120 victim-survivors, secondary victims and others came forward
cases.who: Victorian Department of Education; Beaumaris Primary School and 23 other government schools
cases.cover: Board found a culture of covering up child sexual abuse in the Department of Education to protect the system's reputation; a teacher convicted and found guilty of misconduct in the 1980s was moved into administration and banned from teaching for only three years
cases.d: A Victorian Government Board of Inquiry, set up after reports of abuse at Beaumaris Primary School, tabled its final report in Parliament on 6 March 2024. It examined the school from 1960 to 1994 (abuse there was concentrated in 1971–72) and was widened to 23 other government schools. It focused on four teachers, out of six relevant staff, who are believed to have abused more than 100 students, mostly boys aged 9 to 12. The board found the department 'woefully failed to protect children', had no policies for handling allegations or convictions, and covered up abuse. It made nine recommendations, including a parliamentary apology and accountability processes for historical abuse in all state schools.
cases.cite: Board of Inquiry into Historical Child Sexual Abuse in Beaumaris Primary School and Certain Other Government Schools, final report tabled 6 March 2024, as reported by AAP and EducationHQ

cases.n: Queensland — Crime and Misconduct Commission inquiry into abuse of children in foster care, 'Protecting children' (2004)
cases.who: Queensland Department of Families; foster care and child protection system
cases.d: In May 2003 a woman told a Department of Families office that she had been sexually and physically abused for 13 years in foster care by an approved foster carer and the family's visitors, and that other children placed there were also abused. The Premier referred the system's failures to the Crime and Misconduct Commission, which audited abuse notifications against current carers and held public hearings from 13 October 2003. Its report, released in January 2004, found the department's response 'completely inadequate' at most of nine points where children could have been protected, and concluded that the child protection system had failed Queensland children. It made 110 recommendations, including creating a separate Department of Child Safety and a Child Guardian.
cases.cite: Crime and Misconduct Commission (Queensland), 'Protecting children: an inquiry into abuse of children in foster care', January 2004 (report summary)

cases.n: Tasmania — Ombudsman's review of claims of abuse in state care, 'Listen to the Children' (2004)
cases.victims_note: 1,848 eligible claimants were accepted by the Abuse in State Care program (2003–2013) that followed the review; this counts all forms of abuse, not only sexual abuse
cases.who: Tasmanian state care: state, church and charitable homes (including Ashley, Rochebank, Clarendon, Kennerley, Glenara and Mt St Canice) and foster care
cases.d: After a former state ward spoke publicly in July 2003 about abuse in state care, the Tasmanian Ombudsman reviewed claims from adults who had been abused as children in state care, publishing 'Listen to the Children' in November 2004 and a Phase 2 final report in June 2006. The review covered state, church and charitable homes and foster care, where sexual abuse from the 1950s to the 1970s had been described. It led to the state's Abuse in State Care program (2003–2013), which accepted 1,848 claimants and paid between $35,000 and $60,000 each. Claimants who accepted a payment had to waive future legal action against the government. Tasmania's 2023 Commission of Inquiry later found that allegations against staff and carers revealed through the program had not been acted on.
cases.cite: Ombudsman Tasmania, 'Listen to the Children: Review of Claims of Abuse from Adults in State Care as Children', November 2004 (CLAN library catalogue); Victorian Government redress research summary (2022); Tasmanian Times; Canberra Times on the 2023 Commission of Inquiry

cases.n: Anglican Church of Australia — Parkinson study of reported child sexual abuse, 17 dioceses (2009)
cases.victims_note: 180 complainants in 191 reported cases, 1990–2008; the report describes them as reports, not confirmed incidents
cases.who: Anglican Church of Australia (17 of 23 dioceses)
cases.d: The Anglican Church of Australia's Professional Standards Commission asked for this study after the 2004 General Synod; University of Sydney researchers Patrick Parkinson, Kim Oates and Amanda Jayakody published it in May 2009. It counted 191 cases of alleged child sexual abuse reported to 17 of the 23 dioceses between 1990 and 2008, made by 180 complainants against 135 people. Nearly two-thirds of the accused were clergy or candidates for ordination, about three-quarters of complainants were male, and on average 23 years passed between the abuse and the complaint. Eight percent of cases were never investigated; of 44 cases known to have gone to court, 53% ended in conviction.
cases.cite: P. Parkinson, K. Oates, A. Jayakody, 'Study of Reported Child Sexual Abuse in the Anglican Church', commissioned by the Professional Standards Commission of the General Synod of the Anglican Church of Australia, May 2009

cases.n: New Zealand — Confidential Listening and Assistance Service final report, 'Some memories never fade' (2015)
cases.victims_note: 1,103 participants who were in state care before 1992; abuse heard included physical, sexual, emotional and verbal abuse and neglect
cases.who: New Zealand state care: residential special education, health and welfare institutions
cases.d: The New Zealand Government set up the Confidential Listening and Assistance Service, chaired by Judge Carolyn Henwood, in 2008 to hear people who had been abused or neglected in state care before 1992. It heard 1,103 participants and closed in June 2015; its final report, 'Some memories never fade', became public in August 2015. The panel described 'an alarming amount of abuse and neglect, with extreme levels of violence', including sexual abuse, across the 50 years before 1992, and said much of it was preventable with better oversight. Its work fed into the later Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care.
cases.cite: Confidential Listening and Assistance Service, 'Some memories never fade: Final Report', 2015 (Department of Internal Affairs); NZ Family Violence Clearinghouse, 27 August 2015

cases.n: Charity Commission statutory inquiry — Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain (Jehovah's Witnesses), 2014–2023
cases.place: Mill Hill, London (Watch Tower Britain headquarters during the inquiry)
cases.who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain; Jehovah's Witness congregations in Britain (now under the Kingdom Hall Trust)
cases.cover: Commission found trustees were not as straightforward or transparent as they should have been about who held safeguarding responsibility; repeated legal challenges 'substantially constrained' the inquiry (insufficient evidence of deliberate obstruction)
cases.d: The Charity Commission for England and Wales opened a statutory inquiry into the national Jehovah's Witness charity in May 2014 over its safeguarding policy, after a 2007 inquiry into a London congregation found it had no child protection policy and the NSPCC found in 2013 that the national policy conflicted with UK law and guidance. Watch Tower challenged the inquiry in the courts; the Supreme Court refused it permission to appeal in December 2016, and a tribunal judge said its delays created 'ongoing risks' to children. The Commission's report of 4 August 2023 closed the inquiry because responsibility for safeguarding in more than 1,000 congregations had passed to the Kingdom Hall Trust, which it placed under a compliance case. Jehovah's Witness organisations had reported 67 allegations of child sexual abuse against 67 people for 2009–2019 to IICSA.
cases.cite: Charity Commission for England and Wales, 'Charity inquiry: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain', 4 August 2023; Civil Society News, 4 August 2023

cases.n: Rotherham — IOPC Operation Linden report on South Yorkshire Police (2022)
cases.cover: IOPC found significant failures by South Yorkshire Police to protect children from organised grooming; 8 officers had a case to answer for misconduct and 6 for gross misconduct; 43 complaints upheld
cases.d: The Independent Office for Police Conduct published its Operation Linden report on 22 June 2022, after 91 investigations (begun 2014–2018) into South Yorkshire Police's response to child sexual exploitation in Rotherham from 1997 to 2013. The investigations covered 265 allegations from 51 complainants, 44 of them survivors, and 47 officers. Eight officers had a case to answer for misconduct and six for gross misconduct; five retired officers received sanctions and one misconduct case was found not proven in 2022. The IOPC found the force was not equipped to deal with organised grooming at the scale it met in Rotherham and failed to protect vulnerable children.
cases.cite: Independent Office for Police Conduct, 'The Operation Linden Report', 22 June 2022

cases.n: South Yorkshire — Drew review of South Yorkshire Police's handling of child sexual exploitation (2016)
cases.d: South Yorkshire's Police and Crime Commissioner, Alan Billings, commissioned Professor John Drew to review the force's handling of child sexual exploitation after concerns that Sheffield had seen failings similar to Rotherham's. The review, published on 23 March 2016, found the force had confronted 'a raft of weaknesses' in its earlier approach and had made strong progress over the previous three years. Drew said his picture was incomplete because he could not examine about 200 IPCC complaints about officers linked to Rotherham or speak to witnesses in ongoing criminal cases. At the time, 124 people had been charged with child sexual exploitation offences since the 2014 Jay report.
cases.cite: Independent review of South Yorkshire Police's handling of child sexual exploitation (Drew Review), commissioned by the South Yorkshire Police and Crime Commissioner, 23 March 2016, as reported by the Sheffield Telegraph

notes:
Scope: leftover items from expand_americas_oceania.json and expand_uk_ie_nordic.json (Australia, New Zealand, Pacific, US states, UK grooming reviews, Charity Commission Watch Tower inquiry).

Already on the map and already in another expand file's checklist, so NOT repeated here: Forde Inquiry (aus-forde-inquiry), Tasmanian Commission of Inquiry 2023 (aus-tasmania-coi), Abuse in Care RC 'Beautiful Children' Lake Alice (nzl-lake-alice) and 'Whanaketia' (nzl-whanaketia), SBC Guidepost (usa-sbc-guidepost), Boy Scouts of America (usa-boy-scouts), Penn State Freeh (usa-penn-state-sandusky), Michigan State/Nassar (usa-nassar, plus x-usa-doj-oig-fbi-nassar-2021 and x-usa-usopc-ropes-gray-2018 in expand_americas_oceania.json).
NZ Royal Commission: its published reports are Tāwharautia interim report (Dec 2020), He Purapura Ora he Māra Tipu redress report (2021), Beautiful Children (Lake Alice), Stolen Lives Marked Souls (Marylands) and Whanaketia (2024), plus an administrative report. All are on the map or counted under nzl-whanaketia ('counted once with its interim reports' in expand_americas_oceania.json). No separate checklist items were added for the interim and redress reports to avoid double counting. The RC's reports index (abuseincare.org.nz/reports/) timed out on a permission request; the list comes from the Tāwharautia page's links.

Borderline calls and gaps:
- Tasmanian Ombudsman 2004: the report itself (nla.gov.au) and Find & Connect pages were blocked (bot protection). The record relies on the CLAN catalogue entry (title, date, institutions), the Victorian redress summary (1,848 claimants, $35k–$60k) and the Tasmanian Times (sexual abuse in state care, waiver condition). The share of sexual-abuse claims was not found. victims=1,848 counts all abuse types (explained in victims_note).
- QLD CMC 2004: no count of children sexually abused was in the summary; victims left out.
- Beaumaris: victims=100 is a floor ('more than 100'). Chair not named in the sources opened, so not stated.
- Anglican Parkinson study: status 'acknowledged' (church-commissioned study). The General Synod Professional Standards Commission's own annual reports were not opened and are not listed separately; the Parkinson study is that commission's main published finding. Diocesan boards of inquiry (e.g. Adelaide 2004 Olsson–Chung) are diocesan-commissioned and fail rule 1. Brisbane is on the map as aus-brisbane-hollingworth.
- Debelle (SA) excluded on reach; the lead may prefer to include it as a royal commission on a whole state education department's handling.
- Gordon (WA) excluded on scope, the same as 'Little Children are Sacred'.
- Watch Tower: placed at Mill Hill, London, Watch Tower Britain's headquarters for most of the inquiry. Uses the existing net key 'jehovahs-witnesses' (defined in religious_other.json). The GOV.UK page notes the press release was withdrawn on 10 September 2026 (the report remains the 4 August 2023 publication).
- UK grooming reviews: Derby, Bristol, Kirklees, Peterborough, Calderdale and Bradford reviews all fall below the reach rule (single-city cases with under 30 named victims). The two South Yorkshire items added instead are region-wide or about 100+ victims: IOPC Operation Linden (2022) and the PCC's Drew review (2016). Drew review details come from one press report; the review document itself was not opened.
- Not in my assignment but noticed: the Scottish Parliament Public Petitions Committee 'Report on tackling child sexual exploitation in Scotland' (2014) is a national parliamentary inquiry. It was confirmed only by a library catalogue record (calio.dspacedirect.org/handle/11212/1295) and its findings were not opened, so it was not added. A follow-up could add it. Australian Human Rights Commission 'Forgotten Children' (2014) is still unresearched (listed in expand_americas_oceania.json notes).
- Pacific: no official finding meets the rules for Solomon Islands, Kiribati, CNMI, PNG, Fiji, Tonga or Vanuatu. Solomon Islands (Church of Melanesia study, Makira, 70+ children) and Kiribati (fishing crews, 2003 port ban) could still go on the map as 'reported' cases. The Solomon Islands TRC (2012) covers conflict-era sexual violence against women and girls; it was not opened and is likely out of scope as a primary finding (same call as MMIWG).
- US: Louisiana, New Mexico and New Jersey have investigations but no published finding as of the sources opened (latest: NJ Supreme Court ruling, June 2025). The Archdiocese of Santa Fe and New Orleans bankruptcy settlements were not added (settlements, not findings).
